Question: How does binary search work, and why does it require a sorted list? Answer in one clear short paragraph:
"Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding an item in a sorted list. It works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half until the item is found or located or the search list is empty."The key to this algorithm is that it only needs to look at half of the list. If the list is sorted, then it can be divided into two halves. The first half is searched for the value, and if it's not found, the second half is searched. This process continues until the entire list is searched. In the worst case, the list is already sorted, so we only need to search half of the list. We can also use the fact that the list is sorted to find the middle element, which will be the pivot, and then recursively search on either side of the list. This algorithm has a time complexity of O(n log n) because it requires O(n) comparisons to find the pivot, and it requires O(n) operations to sort the array (O(n) because each element is compared with every other element).
